commitResults.messageBody: Update task parsing and command help to omit slash markers, and play the bundled faaah sound for invalid input.

commitResults.messageTitle: refactor: centralize commands in enum
commitResults.messageBody: Remove the redundant command library and keep command metadata, parsing, and help formatting in CommandType.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor sources to module coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The classes sit in the default package, use `/* */` where Javadoc
belongs, and break the naming, import order and indentation rules. The
banner rows in Serangooner run past the 120 character hard limit, and
`delete` repeats the task number parsing that `updateStatus` already
does.

Let's move every class into a `serangooner` package, replace the old
headers with Javadoc, and bring the layout in line with the standard.
The repeated parsing moves into a single `parseTaskNumber` helper, so
the argument rules for `mark`, `unmark` and `delete` live in one place.

Program output is unchanged. Both the full command set and the argument
error paths were diffed against a build of the previous sources.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: CLAUDE.md: Replace pointer with full rules
commitResults.messageBody:
CLAUDE.md forwards to AGENTS.md, which frames the repository as a
generic starter template and gives the module conventions as bare links.
The commit format, the Java coding standard and the tagging workflow
have to be looked up mid-task, so they get missed.

Let's spell the rules out in CLAUDE.md: project facts, the commit
message convention, the se-education Java standard, the JUnit layout,
the tag-and-push steps, and the AI citation policy. AGENTS.md stays put
as the course's own file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add /done command for milestone release
commitResults.messageBody:
Closing an increment means compiling, reviewing the diff against the
standard, committing, tagging with the exact increment ID, then pushing
the commit and the tag as separate steps. Done by hand this invites a
missed step, and the standing rule against committing unasked has to be
waived each time.

Let's capture the sequence as a slash command taking the tag name as its
argument, mirroring the Codex skill in `.codex/skills/done`. Invoking it
counts as authorisation to commit and push, for that one milestone only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Save and load tasks from the hard disk
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks entered in one session are lost the moment Serangooner exits, so
the list must be rebuilt by hand on every run.

Let's persist the list to ./data/serangooner.txt, reading it when the
list is constructed and writing it back after every edit. TaskList owns
the Storage instance so the file cannot fall out of step with what the
user sees, and each task class encodes its own line so that adding a
task type later needs only one more override.

A line that cannot be understood is skipped and reported in a short
startup message rather than aborting the load, so one damaged line
never costs the user the rest of the list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let each task type read its own saved line
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage both dispatches on the type code and works out where each
field sits, so the layout of a saved line is settled in two places
at once: the task class writes it, and Storage independently reads
it back. Storage also signals a bad line by throwing, which load()
catches purely to count it, even though a damaged line is expected
input rather than a fault.

Let's give each task type a fromSaveFields factory beside its
toSaveFormat, returning an empty optional when the line cannot be
read. Reading and writing then sit together in the class that owns
the format, Storage shrinks to a switch on the type code, and the
load path no longer uses exceptions for ordinary control flow.

A shared readSaveLine helper on Task holds the checks every type
makes, so a saved line is accepted only with the exact field count
expected. A description containing the field separator is therefore
reported as unreadable instead of being loaded back mangled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Store dates and times as date objects
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadlines and events hold their dates as raw text, so the bot cannot
tell a date from any other string handed to it. Nothing can be
compared or filtered, and whatever the user types is echoed straight
back.

Let's parse both into a TaskDateTime, which wraps a LocalDateTime and
remembers whether a time of day was given. Dates are read as
2019-10-15 or 2019-10-15 1800 and shown as 15 Oct 2019 or
20 Oct 2019, 6:00PM, while the save file keeps the input format so a
saved task reads back as the value that was written.

One class owns every formatter, so the two task types share a parser
instead of each growing its own. A date that no longer parses skips
its line on load, joining the unreadable lines the loader already
reports, so one stale date never costs the user the rest of the list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add command to view tasks on or between dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates are held as real dates, but the only way to find what falls on a
given day is to read the whole list by eye. A list that grows past a
screenful makes that impractical.

Let's add "on <date> [to <date>]", which lists the deadlines and
events falling on a single date or touching any date in a range.
Matching goes through Task.isWithin, so each task type decides for
itself what falling within a range means and the command never has to
test what type a task is.

Both listings share one renderer, and it numbers tasks by their
position in the full list, so a number read off a filtered view stays
usable with mark, unmark and delete.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject events that end before they start
commitResults.messageBody:
An event takes any two dates, so one running from 16 Oct to 14 Oct is
stored as written. That event can never be found again: matching looks
for a span running forwards, and a backwards span covers no day at
all, so it answers no date query.

Let's reject the pair when the end falls before the start, comparing
through TaskDateTime so a time of day counts as much as the date. A
saved event whose dates disagree is skipped on load, like any other
line the loader cannot make sense of.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
Extract user interactions into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
The main method decorates the console, runs the command loop and
dispatches commands all at once, while TaskList composes the sentence
reporting what was read from the save file. The wording the user sees is
spread across two classes, and none of it can be exercised without a
real console.

Let's gather every console concern into a Ui class, and have TaskList
report load counts through a LoadReport record that Ui words. Ui takes
its streams through the constructor, so tests can drive it with piped
input and read back what it printed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Move task saving out of TaskList into main class
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList holds a Storage and writes the save file after every edit, so
a list of tasks cannot exist without a file behind it, and its test has
to create a temporary directory just to count tasks. The outcome of a
load is described twice over, by Storage.LoadResult and by
TaskList.LoadReport.

Let's hand TaskList a plain list of tasks and let Serangooner hold the
user interface, the list and the save file together, deciding when a
change is written back. Storage.LoadResult absorbs the error message so
that one class describes one file read.

Saving happens only after a command that can change the list, marked by
CommandType.isMutating. Saving after every command would rewrite the
file on a plain 'list' and destroy any line the load could not read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command parsing into a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Knowledge of how a command is written is spread across four classes:
TaskList slices arguments out of raw command strings, and Deadline and
Event each hold a private parser keyed to a hardcoded offset into the
keyword they belong to. Renaming a keyword means editing a task class,
a list class and the command enum together.

Let's gather every step that turns typed text into meaning into one
Parser class, which hands values to the rest of the program: a command
type, a task, a task number or a range of dates. TaskList takes those
values in place of command strings, so it no longer speaks command
syntax, and the tasks no longer know that a command exists. Offsets
now come from the keyword's own length and error messages from the
command's declared syntax, so a keyword can be reworded in one place.

Parser also trims the line it is given, which repairs a command typed
with a leading space; such a command used to lose a character off the
argument following its keyword.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reduce TaskList to holding the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList carries nearly half the wording the program shows: every edit
returns a finished sentence, and the class renders both listings. Ui
claims in its own header to be the one place such wording lives, and a
list that answers in console prose cannot be handed to a different
kind of interface. The three add methods differ only by the label each
puts in its message.

Let's have every edit give back the task it touched and leave the
wording to Ui. A task now names its own kind, so a single add method
serves all three, and a listing comes back as tasks paired with the
numbers the user knows them by, which keeps a number read off a
filtered listing usable with mark, unmark and delete. The out of range
message stays behind, since the list alone knows its own size.

Drop MAX_TASKS as well. It named a limit that nothing enforced, being
only the initial capacity of the backing list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Task abstract
commitResults.messageBody:
A plain Task can be built, but it is not a whole task: it has no name
for its kind, falls on no date, and writes a save line carrying no type
code. Storage cannot read that line back, so such a task would vanish
on the next load without a word.

Let's make Task abstract, and getTypeName along with it, so that only
the kinds that answer those questions can exist. The constructor turns
protected to match. Nothing built a plain Task, so this closes the gap
before it is ever reached rather than fixing a fault.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add serialVersionUID to SerangoonerException
commitResults.messageBody:
Compiling with -Xlint:all warns that the class is serializable without
a version of its own, which is the last warning the build reports.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Ui the one owner of console output
commitResults.messageBody:
Two things sit on the wrong side of the line between showing something
and being something. CommandType builds the numbered help listing, the
last piece of user-facing rendering outside Ui, and the only reason Ui
still offers a method that prints a string handed to it. Ui in turn
runs afplay in a subprocess, so the class that speaks to the console
also depends on a macOS binary.

Let's have Ui render the help listing from the commands it is given,
which leaves CommandType holding command data alone, and let a
SoundPlayer own the noise, the file it comes from and the thread it
plays on. Ui keeps the decision to make a sound and knows nothing of
how one is made.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command switch with Command objects
commitResults.messageBody:
The main loop switches over a CommandType to decide what to do, then
asks the enum whether the list changed so that it knows to save. A new
command therefore means editing the enum, the switch and the parser
together, and the loop must know what each command needs in order to
call it at all.

Let's have Parser return a Command that already holds everything it
needs, and give every command an execute of its own. The loop reads a
line, runs whatever comes back, and asks only whether to stop. A
command that changes the list saves it, which leaves isMutating with
no one to ask, so it goes.

Saying goodbye is now a command like any other, so the divider that
closes the exchange comes from the loop and showFarewell no longer
draws one of its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-MoreOOP'
Split classes into packages by responsibility
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class sits in one flat serangooner package, so the source layout
says nothing about which classes serve the user, which hold the model
and which touch the disk. It also hides the direction of dependencies.

Let's group them into command, storage, task and ui packages, leaving
the entry point, the parser and the shared exception at the root.
Dependencies then run one way: root to command, command to ui and
storage, both of those to task.

Two references stood against that order and are moved rather than
worked around. DateRange leaves Parser for the task package, so a
command no longer depends on the parser that built it. HelpCommand
words the command list itself and hands Ui plain strings, so ui no
longer depends on command. Storage reads saved tasks through
fromSaveFields, package-private and compiling only because every class
shared a package; it is now public, stating a dependency that was there
all along.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
Point Gradle at the Serangooner entry point
commitResults.messageBody:
The merged Gradle build carries the skeleton's names: it launches
seedu.duke.Duke and packages the fat JAR as duke.jar. Neither class
nor name exists here, so `gradle run` fails outright.

Let's set mainClass to serangooner.Serangooner and name the shadowJar
output serangooner.jar, so the build refers to the bot it actually
produces.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace javac instructions with Gradle
commitResults.messageBody:
The project builds through the Gradle wrapper now, but the notes still
describe Gradle as unmerged and hand out a raw javac line that knows
nothing about the test suite or the packaged JAR. Following them skips
the tests entirely.

Let's document the wrapper tasks instead, and make the increment
checklist ask for a green `./gradlew build` rather than a bare compile.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover the remaining gaps in Storage tests
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage already has tests for loading and saving, but three parts of its
documented contract are unpinned: that a save replaces the file's former
contents rather than appending, that the done flag survives a round trip
for every task type, and that a line carrying extra fields is skipped.

Let's test those three, and record the coverage policy the tests follow
so later classes are judged the same way: the valuable half of a class's
methods earns tests, and a change updates them in the same commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the valuable half of the task package
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList carries tests, but the six classes it holds tasks for do not:
date parsing, the save-line reader, the date-range check behind the
"on" listing and the rule that an event cannot end before it starts are
all unpinned, and they are where the package's real logic lives.

Let's cover those methods per class, leaving getters, setters and plain
overrides untested as the coverage policy allows. TaskList itself gains
the undo ordering and range-boundary cases it was missing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test every non-trivial public method in tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
The task package is tested where the logic is densest, but a handful of
public methods are still unpinned: the base class's own completion
flag and save line, each type's name, and the conversions TaskDateTime
hands out. Nothing guards them against a careless edit.

Let's cover the rest, testing Task through a minimal subclass so the
base class is exercised on its own terms rather than through Todo.
Plain getters and record accessors stay untested.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the rest of the ui package
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui is tested for most of what it prints, but the unmark message, the
successful undo message and the divider are unpinned, as is reading a
command once the input runs out. SoundPlayer has no tests at all.

Let's cover the remaining Ui methods, and pin SoundPlayer's silence
when it is disabled. An enabled player shells out to the system audio
player, so it is left alone rather than made to sound during a test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test every non-trivial public method in commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Each command type has a test that its execute does the happy path, but
the failure paths are thin: only mark is checked for refusing a bad
task number, undo is never followed after a mark or a delete, and no
test says a read-only command must leave the save file alone.
CommandType has no tests at all.

Let's cover those, and pin the enum invariants the parser and the help
listing both lean on: a keyword is unique, lower case and space free,
and each syntax line starts with its own keyword.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the parser and the chatbot itself
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser is tested for the shapes it accepts, but not for the ones it
must refuse: a shouted keyword, a word that merely begins with one, a
task number too large to hold. Serangooner has no tests at all, so
nothing says a command reaches the save file or that bye ends the loop.

Let's fill in the parser's edges, and drive Serangooner through its own
run loop over stood-in standard streams. Only accepted input is fed to
it, since an error would set off the sound player.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Close the depth gaps left in the test suite
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class already carries tests, yet some of them pass against code
that is subtly wrong. A filtered listing is only ever checked with a
full list, where a task's number happens to equal its position, so a
listing that renumbered from one would go unnoticed even though the
numbers it prints must stay usable with mark and delete.

Let's cover the cases that separate correct code from merely plausible
code: a description carrying the end separator ahead of the start one,
an edit refused after a successful one, a task restored to the position
it was deleted from, and a listing that keeps the numbers of the full
list. Each was confirmed by mutating the method it covers and checking
that the test fails.

A description carrying the field separator still costs the user that
task on the next load. That behaviour is pinned as a test rather than
fixed, alongside the lenient dates and the splitting the suite already
records.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
Document how to run the packaged JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
The README still hands out a raw javac line that predates the Gradle
wrapper. Following it builds without the test suite and never reaches
the packaged JAR at all. It also says nothing to the reader who
downloaded that JAR from a release rather than cloning the source,
which is now the way most people will meet serangooner.

Let's give both readers what they need: the steps for running the
released JAR in a folder of its own, where the save file ends up, and
the wrapper tasks that produce the JAR in the first place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command for searching descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Picking a task out of the list means reading the whole thing by eye,
which stops being workable as soon as the list outgrows a screen. The
one filter serangooner offers narrows by date, so a task carrying no
date cannot be narrowed down at all.

Let's add a find command that keeps only the tasks whose description
carries a keyword. The search goes through the same filter the date
range already uses, so a match keeps the number it holds in the full
list and stays usable with mark, unmark and delete. Case is ignored:
a keyword is free text the user wrote themselves, possibly weeks ago,
and the case it was written in is not worth remembering.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Checkstyle to the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard is enforced by eye alone, so a style slip is only
caught when someone notices it in review.

Let's run Checkstyle as part of the build, using the se-edu rule set
that encodes the same standard we already follow. Wiring it into
`check` means `./gradlew build` fails on a violation, which catches the
slip before it reaches a diff rather than after.

The main source already complied. The test source needed three
cosmetic corrections to pass, none of which change behaviour: a wrapped
line may not open with `(`, so the lambda in `assertThrows` now trails
the call line; one unused import is gone; and a test method with three
underscore-separated parts is renamed to the two the standard allows.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename identifiers to follow the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Several names do not follow the naming rules of the coding standard.
Methods such as entries(), matching() and argumentOf() are not verbs;
readSaveLine() names a line while taking already-split fields;
SAVE_FIELDS holds a count rather than a collection; and the separator
constants share a suffix where the standard asks for a prefix.

A name that misdescribes what it refers to gets read wrongly, and a
reader who misreads a name misreads the code around it.

Let's,
* rename the non-verb methods so that they name their action
* rename Event's from/to fields to startDateTime/endDateTime
* give the associated separator constants a shared prefix
* rename the vague file, label and f variables to say what they hold
* update the tests, including test names carrying a renamed feature

Each new name reuses vocabulary already present nearby, so that
related things keep looking related: parseSaveFields sits beside
Parser.parse*, and getEntriesWithin beside Task.isWithin.

Nothing changes behavior: the user-facing wording and the save file
format are untouched, which is why the tests needed only the renames.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ui: Return messages instead of printing them
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui both chooses the wording and writes it to a stream, and every
command reports its outcome by calling a show method on it. The words
and the console they land on are therefore one thing.

A second interface cannot reuse any of that wording without also
inheriting a PrintStream it has no use for, and a command's outcome is
unavailable to anything but the stream it was printed to.

Let's split the two apart:

* turn each Ui show method into a format method returning its message
* move the reading, the printing, the banner and the dividers into a
  new Console class beside it
* have Command#execute return the message rather than print it

The banner and the dividers go to Console rather than Ui because they
are console furniture: an interface that separates turns some other
way has no use for either.

Each command now saves before composing its reply, so a task whose
save fails no longer reports success first.

The console output is unchanged, byte for byte: a session of fifteen
commands, error cases included, produces identical output before and
after.

UiTest loses its streams and asserts on the returned strings; the
reading and printing tests move to a new ConsoleTest.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Serangooner: Answer one line at a time
commitResults.messageBody:
Answering a line and reading the next one are tangled together in
run(): the loop parses, runs the command, prints the outcome and
catches the failure, all in place.

A chat window has to do the same work, but it is handed a line by a
button rather than by a Scanner, and it shows the answer in a bubble
rather than on a stream. It cannot reuse run() without also inheriting
the console.

Let's pull answering out of the loop:

* add getResponse(String), which parses and runs one line and returns
  what to say back
* return it as a Response record carrying the text, whether the line
  ended the conversation, and whether it was refused
* add getGreeting() and getLoadReport() for what is said before the
  first line is typed
* leave run() as the console's caller of those

Refusals come back as a Response rather than an exception, because an
interface that stays open after a bad command should not have to catch
one to keep going. The isError flag lets it tell a refusal apart from
an answer without reading the wording.

A no-argument constructor is added because JavaFX builds an
Application through one.

The console output is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a chat window built with JavaFX
commitResults.messageBody:
Serangooner is reachable only through a terminal. Typing at a prompt
asks the user to keep the exchange in their head, and it gives a
passer-by no idea what the program can do.

Let's put a chat window in front of it:

* add the JavaFX dependencies for all three platforms, as the module
  tutorial gives them, and start the program from a Launcher
* describe the window and a message bubble in FXML under
  resources/view, with the styling in resources/css
* add a serangooner.gui package holding the two controllers behind
  those files, Main and the Launcher

The window asks Serangooner#getResponse for each line, so it shares
the parser, the task list and the wording with the terminal and can
add nothing of its own to what the chatbot says.

gui sits above the root package rather than inside serangooner.ui,
because it has to name Serangooner and the ui package may not.

A reply is shown mirrored against the message that prompted it, a
refused command is tinted and keeps the sound the terminal plays, and
bye closes the window once the farewell has been read.

The terminal interface is untouched and still starts from
serangooner.Serangooner.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: README: Say how to start each interface
commitResults.messageBody:
The instructions describe running the jar without saying that a window
now opens, and they do not mention that the terminal interface is
still there.

A reader following them will be surprised by the window, and has no
way of discovering that the same commands can be piped in from a
shell.

Let's say that the jar opens a chat window, and add the command that
starts the terminal interface instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-GUI'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a JavaFX chat window as a second way to talk to Serangooner,
alongside the terminal interface, which stays as it was.

Ui now composes messages and returns them rather than printing them,
so both interfaces share one vocabulary, and Serangooner answers one
line at a time so both can ask for those answers the same way.
